title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature
authors: Xuanlyu Zhu, Feng Tian, Yang Zhong, Pengqi Zheng, Xiwen Bi, Ling Luo
abstract: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.

infographic.key_insight: The best system linked phenotype concepts to specific patients in full-text biomedical articles with an overall score of 0.7389, beating the baseline by 8.37 percentage points.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Patient-specific phenotype extraction could support rare disease research and genotype–phenotype analysis, but clinical utility was not evaluated.
method: Recognize phenotype concepts in full-text biomedical literature.
Associate phenotype concepts with individual patients.
Top teams explored biomedical language models, LLMs, and ensemble strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The evaluation used 200 annotated PatientPheX articles covering 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient–phenotype associations.
infographic.watch_item: Patient attribution and phenotype normalization remain challenging, particularly in articles describing multiple patients.
infographic.paper_title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature

title: Visualizing and Interpreting Temporal Care Team Dynamics for Cancer Survival Risk Analysis
authors: Yuhua Huang, Hsiao-Ying Lu, Kwan-Liu Ma
abstract: Cancer care is a longitudinal, time-sensitive process requiring coordination among diverse healthcare professionals (HCPs), whose collaboration evolves throughout treatment. Prior studies link care team structure to patient outcomes, but the temporal dynamics of collaboration and their relationship to evolving patient risk remain poorly understood. We introduce a visual analytics framework for modeling and interpreting time-varying care team interactions in oncology. We construct dynamic collaboration networks from electronic health record (EHR)-mediated communication data and use a temporal graph neural network (TGNN) to estimate patient outcome risk over time. We then investigate how changes in care team composition and specialist participation relate to shifts in estimated risk across treatment stages. Our multi-view interactive system combines TGNN-based risk modeling with coordinated visualizations of care team networks, feature-level explanations from a surrogate logistic regression model, and exploratory what-if analysis. Without making causal claims, the system helps analysts examine how risk estimates co-evolve with collaboration patterns and identify care team characteristics associated with these changes. We demonstrate its utility through expert-guided analysis scenarios involving 505 patients with breast, colorectal, and lung cancers, evaluating its ability to reveal clinically meaningful collaboration patterns. This work improves the interpretability of temporal graph-based models in longitudinal, team-based healthcare, with potential applicability to other evolving collaborative settings.

infographic.key_insight: A visual analytics framework links evolving cancer care team interactions with model-estimated patient risk, enabling exploration without implying causation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system may help researchers and care teams investigate how collaboration patterns relate to changing risk estimates during cancer treatment.
method: Build dynamic care team networks from EHR-mediated communications.
Estimate patient outcome risk over time using a temporal graph neural network.
Explore networks, surrogate logistic regression explanations, and what-if scenarios through coordinated visualizations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Expert-guided analysis scenarios involved 505 patients with breast, colorectal, and lung cancers; the abstract reports no quantitative predictive performance.
infographic.watch_item: Observed associations and exploratory what-if results do not establish that changing team composition would improve patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Visualizing and Interpreting Temporal Care Team Dynamics for Cancer Survival Risk Analysis

title: Multimodal Generative AI Assists Comprehensive Echocardiographic Interpretation
authors: Yi Qin, Marawan Elbatel, Shanshan Song, Taoran Huang, Jiarong Guo, Ningshu Li
abstract: Echocardiography is the cornerstone of cardiovascular diagnostics, yet its global utility is constrained by a critical shortage of experienced interpreters. Current artificial intelligence (AI) solutions remain limited, typically operating as opaque "black boxes" or focusing on narrow tasks that fail to capture the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning of a clinician. Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal vision-language model that performs comprehensive echocardiographic analysis to support clinician interpretation. By emulating the cognitive workflow of a cardiologist, EchoChat integrates vast medical knowledge with a chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to explicitly ground its conclusions in visual evidence. Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations, our model establishes a new state-of-the-art across diverse cohorts from six international medical centers. It supports the broadest diagnostic scope of 33 cardiac conditions and findings, including 15 newly added conditions for which it achieves an average F1 of 73.7% across available external evaluations. It surpasses existing best-performing foundation models in cardiac condition recognition (improving average recall by 13.54% on shared tasks) and quantification (average R2 score increase of 0.275 on shared tasks). Furthermore, in a source-blinded echocardiographer reader study, echocardiography reports co-generated with EchoChat were rated higher in diagnostic accuracy and completeness by two senior echocardiographers, and improved diagnostic performance from 72.78% to 82.75% in terms of F1 score over routine-reader only reports. These results demonstrate that integrating clinical reasoning into multimodal AI can democratize specialist expertise and transform the standard of cardiovascular care.

infographic.key_insight: EchoChat is a multimodal generative AI model that supports comprehensive echocardiographic interpretation across 33 cardiac conditions and findings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: AI-assisted reports achieved higher diagnostic F1 than routine-reader-only reports in a reader study, suggesting potential to support clinicians facing interpretation workloads.
method: Trained on echocardiography–instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations.
Combines echocardiographic visual inputs with medical knowledge and explicit reasoning intended to ground conclusions in visual evidence.
Evaluated condition recognition, quantitative measurements, and clinician–AI co-generated reports.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across cohorts from six international centers, EchoChat achieved 73.7% average F1 for 15 newly added conditions in available external evaluations; reader-study diagnostic F1 increased from 72.78% to 82.75% with AI assistance.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective real-world safety or patient-outcome benefits; generated reasoning and findings require clinician verification.
infographic.paper_title: Multimodal Generative AI Assists Comprehensive Echocardiographic Interpretation

title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Ronald Fecso, José Morano, Botond Fazekas, Paul Widmann-Sedlnitzky, Dorota Himel, Laetita Hinterhuber
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Retinal OCT finding recognition does not ensure accurate localization: RetGrounder improved grounding F1 from 23.7% to 33.9%, but performance remained limited.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Localizing reported retinal abnormalities is important for assessing whether AI image interpretations are grounded in visible evidence.
method: Created RetinaGroundBench with ophthalmologist-annotated retinal OCT scans.
Introduced AggIoU to evaluate combined coverage from overlapping predicted boxes.
Evaluated 27 open-source MLLMs and fine-tuned the 8B RetGrounder using OCT grounding and textual information.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark contains 815 B-scans and 4,537 bounding boxes spanning 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases; RetGrounder achieved a 43% relative grounding F1 improvement over the best general-purpose model.
infographic.watch_item: Grounding performance remains limited, and these benchmark results do not establish safety or effectiveness in clinical practice.
infographic.paper_title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models

title: The Value of System 1 Models in Medicine
authors: Xiufeng Yang, Konstantinos Vrettos, Zeineb Ben Chaaben, Fabian Drexel, Jannik Lübberstedt, Johannes Moll
abstract: Many clinical decisions are a choice among a few fixed options, taken quickly and in large numbers. Such decisions also need an uncertainty estimate to know when to defer to a clinician. Generative language models answer slowly in free text and state their confidence poorly. In contrast, System 1 models answer zero-shot with a probability for each answer. However, their performance across clinical tasks is unknown. Four System 1 models, two proprietary and two with open weights, were evaluated zero-shot on 86 public tasks from 14 clinical domains in 20 languages, spanning examination questions and medical imaging. Tasks were assigned to six capability tiers before analysis. The primary outcome was the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary outcomes included calibration, language effects and comparisons with published results and generative models. Across 179,111 cases, the mean AUROC of the best model per task was 0.94 for medical knowledge, 0.93 for text understanding, 0.83 for clinical judgement from text, 0.89 for image perception, 0.84 for 2D image findings and 0.69 for volumetric findings. Imaging tasks scored 0.09 (95% CI, 0.06 to 0.11) lower than text tasks (P < 0.001). The best model matched or exceeded the best published result on 13 of 26 text tasks and on 8 of 35 imaging tasks. Triage nurses outperformed the best model (accuracy, 0.85 vs. 0.56). One decision took 0.34 to 0.44 seconds and 24 to 81 joules on open-weight models run locally. Accuracy on identical questions fell by up to 39 percentage points from English to Yoruba. Generative models of the same family were 11 to 76 times slower, with 3 to 5 percentage points higher balanced accuracy. System 1 models decide quickly, cheaply and with usable confidence when the answer is stated in a text or recalled from medical knowledge, but not when it must be judged or read from an image.

infographic.key_insight: System 1 models made fast, probability-scored decisions but performed best on medical knowledge and text understanding, with weaker results on clinical judgement and volumetric imaging.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These models may warrant further evaluation for narrowly defined clinical tasks, but speed and confidence scores do not establish safe autonomous use.
method: Evaluated four models zero-shot on 86 public tasks across 14 clinical domains and 20 languages.
Grouped tasks into six capability tiers and used AUROC as the primary outcome.
Assessed calibration, language effects, speed and comparisons with published results and generative models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 179,111 cases, mean AUROC for the best model per task ranged from 0.94 for medical knowledge to 0.69 for volumetric findings; imaging scored 0.09 below text tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance varied substantially by task and language: triage nurses outperformed the best model, and accuracy on identical questions fell by up to 39 percentage points from English to Yoruba.
infographic.paper_title: The Value of System 1 Models in Medicine

title: From Structured Records to Patient Narratives: Preserving Clinical Alignment in LLM-Generated Health Summaries
authors: Bayram Ayadi, Florian Geissler, Johanna Schmidhuber
abstract: As wearable and digital health systems increasingly generate longitudinal physiological records, communicating these observations in patient-accessible language remains a significant challenge. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising mechanism for translating structured clinical information into readable narratives, but this process may introduce semantic drift, where clinically precise meaning is distorted during simplification. We investigate evidence-grounded health summarization for menstrual health monitoring using a constrained generation framework that combines structured evidence conditioning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using a prompt-based constrained generation framework. We evaluate semantic alignment using Natural Language Inference (NLI), atomic factuality metrics, and readability measures. Across three LLMs and 4,500 generated summaries, explicit grounding constraints consistently improve clinical alignment, particularly by improving uncertainty preservation and, once faithfulness is evaluated against retrieved evidence, generally preserving or improving faithfulness, while effects on omission remain model-dependent. We also find that improved clinical alignment comes at the cost of increased reading difficulty and medical terminology. These findings highlight the need to jointly evaluate faithfulness, uncertainty preservation, and readability when developing patient-facing medical LLM systems.

infographic.key_insight: Explicit evidence-grounding constraints improved clinical alignment in LLM-generated menstrual health summaries, but made them harder to read.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Patient-facing summaries need to preserve clinical meaning and uncertainty while remaining understandable.
method: Generated narratives from structured menstrual health records.
Combined retrieval-augmented generation with prompt-based grounding constraints.
Evaluated alignment using natural language inference, atomic factuality metrics, and readability measures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three LLMs and 4,500 summaries, constraints improved uncertainty preservation and generally preserved or improved faithfulness when assessed against retrieved evidence, while omission effects varied by model.
infographic.watch_item: Greater alignment came with increased reading difficulty and medical terminology, highlighting a trade-off for patient-facing implementation.
infographic.paper_title: From Structured Records to Patient Narratives: Preserving Clinical Alignment in LLM-Generated Health Summaries

title: Natural Language Processing Based Solution for Labeling Brain Metastasis Identified in Radiology Reports
authors: Liu, T.; Han, Y. T.; Zuo, H.; Das, S.; Lin, H.-M.; Colak, E.; Istasy, M.; Ladak, A. M.; Bigenimana, J. C.; Gondara, L.; Simkin, J.; Lee, J.; Roozbeh, D.; Nichol, A. M.; Easaw, J.; Walker, E.; Yip, S.; Mou, L.; Yuan, Y.
abstract: PurposeBrain metastases (BM) far exceed primary CNS tumours and constitute the majority workload for neuro-oncology care providers. Currently, the cancer registries only capture synchronous BMs, which is only a small proportion of all BMs. We aim to develop and validate a natural language processing (NLP) algorithm that identifies brain metastases in radiology reports, enabling scalable surveillance of asynchronous BMs. MethodsUsing population-based cancer registry data in Alberta, Canada, we identified a cancer cohort diagnosed between 2012-2019 with follow-up to 2022. All brain/head radiology reports at and post-cancer diagnosis were identified. Reports were sampled through a multi-phase approach and manually labeled for BM presence. We trained two Bio_ClinicalBERT models on the "Findings" and "Impressions" sections, respectively, and took the maximum predicted probability as the report-level prediction. Internal and external validation used reports from the Canadian provinces of Alberta, Ontario, and British Columbia. ResultsThe models were trained on 1,879 samples. For internal validation, 1,833 reports from 357 patients were tested. At a probability threshold of 0.4, the model achieved a sensitivity of 0.888 and precision of 0.499. The ensemble substantially outperformed single-section models, which achieved sensitivities of only 67.8% (Findings) and 74.2% (Impressions). On external validation, sensitivity was 0.918 in Ontario and 0.726 in British Columbia, demonstrating robustness across diverse data distributions. ConclusionsAn NLP-based pipeline processing both Findings and Impressions sections has been developed and validated in three Canadian provinces. It meets cancer registry operational requirements and to be implemented into the surveillance workflow in Alberta and British Columbia, providing a foundation for population-level BM surveillance.

infographic.key_insight: Combining NLP predictions from radiology Findings and Impressions identified brain metastases with higher sensitivity than either section alone.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The pipeline could support cancer registry surveillance of brain metastases diagnosed after the initial cancer diagnosis, which current registries often miss.
method: Manually labeled brain/head radiology reports from a population-based Alberta cancer cohort.
Trained two Bio_ClinicalBERT models on 1,879 samples, separately analyzing Findings and Impressions.
Used the higher section-level probability as the report prediction and validated across three Canadian provinces.
infographic.evidence_signal: Internal validation on 1,833 reports from 357 patients yielded 88.8% sensitivity and 49.9% precision at a 0.4 threshold; external sensitivity was 91.8% in Ontario and 72.6% in British Columbia.
infographic.watch_item: Modest precision and variable external sensitivity warrant local validation and a review workflow before registry implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Natural Language Processing Based Solution for Labeling Brain Metastasis Identified in Radiology Reports

title: EigenGradCAM with AugSmooth: Enhancing Explainability and Precision in Multi-Stage Alzheimer's Disease Detection
authors: Arsham Azam, Sagar Ashraf, Tayyaba Farhat, Rasikh Ali, Sheeraz Akram
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurological disorder associated with memory loss, cognitive decline, and behavioral disturbances. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential, yet MRI-based deep learning models often lack interpretability, limiting their clinical use. This study presents an explainable deep learning approach for four-class AD staging using 2D axial MRI images. The method combines eigenvector-based Grad-CAM with gradient smoothing to improve saliency localization and heatmap stability. Principal component analysis is applied to gradient-weighted convolutional layers, while Gaussian noise is added to saliency weights before decomposition. To address class imbalance in the Moderate Dementia category, Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) generates synthetic samples to balance the four-stage training distribution. Custom convolutional neural networks are trained on the Best Alzheimer MRI Dataset, achieving 97.2% test accuracy, 97.0% balanced accuracy, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.944. The area under the ROC curve ranges from 0.96 to 0.99 across classes. Generated heatmaps highlight the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, regions associated with Alzheimer's disease biomarkers. These findings suggest that the proposed approach combines strong classification performance with improved model interpretability, although further clinical validation is needed.

infographic.key_insight: EigenGradCAM with AugSmooth pairs four-class Alzheimer's MRI classification with more stable saliency maps highlighting disease-associated brain regions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach may help researchers interpret MRI model predictions, but its suitability for clinical diagnosis remains unvalidated.
method: Train custom CNNs on 2D axial MRI images for four-class staging.
Use WGAN-GP synthetic samples to address Moderate Dementia class imbalance.
Combine eigenvector-based Grad-CAM, principal component analysis, and Gaussian-noise smoothing to generate heatmaps.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the Best Alzheimer MRI Dataset, the study reports 97.2% test accuracy, 97.0% balanced accuracy, MCC of 0.944, and class-level ROC AUCs of 0.96–0.99.
infographic.watch_item: Further clinical validation is needed; highlighted brain regions alone do not establish that predictions are clinically reliable.
infographic.paper_title: EigenGradCAM with AugSmooth: Enhancing Explainability and Precision in Multi-Stage Alzheimer's Disease Detection

title: MedCaseAgent: From Multimodal Clinical Evidence to Rare Disease Case Reports
authors: Hongkang Chu, Yifan Shen, Tianjiao Yu, Zhuoqing Zhong, Jianguo Cao, Meihuan Huang
abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in clinical documentation, generating the rigorous, evidence-based reasoning required for unprecedented, atypical, and rare disease case reports remains a significant challenge. We present MedCaseAgent, an end-to-end agentic reasoning paradigm that bridges this gap by synthesizing publication-quality reports from unstructured clinical notes. MedCaseAgent leverages a hierarchical structure, integrating patient-level data mining with iterative, tool-integrated reasoning. By dynamically querying medical literature and knowledge bases, the agent maintains high clinical fidelity and assesses case novelty. The framework is inherently modular, supporting various backbone LLMs in a plug-and-play fashion. To facilitate this research, we release MedCase-150K, a large-scale multimodal clinical case-report corpus, and MedCase-Bench, a robust temporally held-out evaluation suite. We also introduce an open-source model post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B and optimized specifically for this task. Under both LLM-judged and rule-based evaluation, MedCaseAgent outperforms existing general-purpose and specialized medical LLMs and agents. Blinded expert reviews and ablations further support the system's clinical relevance and evidence grounding.

infographic.key_insight: MedCaseAgent combines clinical data mining with literature-grounded AI reasoning to generate case-report drafts for rare, atypical, and previously unreported presentations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support evidence-based case-report preparation, but the abstract does not establish safety or effectiveness for clinical decision-making.
method: Hierarchical processing of unstructured, multimodal patient evidence.
Iterative reasoning with medical literature and knowledge-base queries to assess evidence and case novelty.
Modular LLM backbones, including a task-specific model post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors introduce MedCase-150K and temporally held-out MedCase-Bench, reporting gains over general-purpose and medical LLMs and agents with LLM-judged and rule-based evaluation, alongside supportive blinded expert reviews and ablations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical performance or error rates; generated claims, citations, and novelty assessments still require expert verification.
infographic.paper_title: MedCaseAgent: From Multimodal Clinical Evidence to Rare Disease Case Reports

title: GWDM: A Guided Wavelet Diffusion Model for Realistic Histopathology Image Generation
authors: Abdullah, Tao Huang, Ickjai Lee, Lei Bi, Euijoon Ahn
abstract: Histopathology images are recognized as a reliable and comprehensive modality for Deep Learning (DL) based diagnosis. However, effectiveness is constrained by limited large-scale annotated datasets, as collecting expert-labeled medical data is costly and time-intensive. Recent advances in generative models, particularly diffusion models, demonstrate strong capabilities in synthesizing medically relevant content for dataset augmentation. Existing generative frameworks treat histopathology patches as generic natural images, failing to enforce biological constraints such as histomorphological structures and heterogeneous staining patterns essential for valid synthesis. We propose a guided wavelet diffusion model (GWDM) framework that captures image details at multiple scales using wavelets and leverages controllable conditioning based on domain-specific histopathological features (e.g., tissue patterns and color variations). We further formulate a histomorphological guidance loss applied to real and generated patches. A loss ramping strategy gradually introduces these constraints during training, ensuring stable optimization and robust modeling of tissue architecture. GWDM was evaluated on three benchmark datasets (BCSS, MoNuSeg, and PAIP2019), consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative methods. Ablation studies confirmed that domain-guided conditioning, perceptual loss, and structural similarity loss each contribute meaningfully to synthesis quality. Downstream nuclei and tissue segmentation experiments further validated the clinical utility of GWDM-generated images, demonstrating consistent performance improvements when synthetic data augments real training sets. This work shows that domain-specific conditioning and dual-loss optimization generate realistic histopathology patches, reducing data scarcity and improving clinical downstream segmentation performance.

infographic.key_insight: GWDM combines wavelet-based diffusion with histopathology-specific guidance to generate realistic tissue patches for training-data augmentation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Synthetic patches improved downstream nuclei and tissue segmentation in benchmark experiments, suggesting potential value for research on data-limited pathology AI.
method: Use wavelets to capture image details at multiple scales.
Condition generation on tissue patterns and staining variations.
Gradually introduce histomorphological guidance losses to stabilize training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across BCSS, MoNuSeg, and PAIP2019, the authors report stronger generation performance than state-of-the-art comparators and improved segmentation when synthetic images augment real training data.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative effect sizes or external clinical validation, so real-world benefit and generalization remain uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: GWDM: A Guided Wavelet Diffusion Model for Realistic Histopathology Image Generation

title: IndoNutriQA: An Indonesian Clinical Nutrition Question Answering Benchmark
authors: Tirana Noor Fatyanosa, Ummu Ditya Erliana, Mahendra Data, Muhammad Nurwegiono, Eleazar Tadeo Eman, Alham Fikri Aji
abstract: Clinical Question Answering (QA) underpins Clinical Intelligent Decision Support Systems, but progress is severely limited for low-resource languages such as Indonesian by the absence of public domain-specific data. We introduce IndoNutriQA, an expert-curated Indonesian clinical QA benchmark of 911 question-answer pairs built from real clinical-nutrition reports. Rather than a large-scale training corpus, it is positioned as a high-quality evaluation resource: every pair is grounded in a clinically relevant context, enriched with structured metadata (anthropometric assessment, medical diagnosis, document provenance, chunk segmentation). Eight standardised question types following the Nutrition Care Process (NCP), including the Problem, Etiology, Sign and Symptom (PES) diagnosis statement, are answered for every report, which was written by a graduate-level dietetic intern, by one of three nutritionists. Answers are free-form clinical prose rather than extractive spans, and an expert validation study finds 6-10% of reference answers contestable. The dataset supports generative, extractive and retrieval-augmented QA as well as zero- and few-shot LLM evaluation. We report fine-tuned baselines (IndoBERT variants, mT5, RAG) with 5-fold cross-validation, learning curves and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and benchmark eight contemporary LLMs zero- and five-shot. We further calibrate our LLM-as-judge rubric against three expert raters (one RD, two nutritionists), finding it human-comparable on factuality and completeness but unreliable on clinical safety, and a human error analysis shows it misses unsupported content that the raters identify. IndoNutriQA is released to foster research in Indonesian clinical NLP and nutritional decision support.

infographic.key_insight: IndoNutriQA introduces an expert-curated benchmark for evaluating Indonesian clinical nutrition question answering in a low-resource language.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark supports research toward Indonesian nutrition decision support but does not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Curated 911 question–answer pairs from real clinical-nutrition reports, with clinical context and structured metadata.
Used eight standardized Nutrition Care Process question types with free-form answers provided by nutritionists.
Evaluated fine-tuned QA models and eight LLMs, and calibrated an LLM judge against three expert raters.

infographic.watch_item: The LLM judge was unreliable for clinical safety and missed unsupported content identified by human raters.
infographic.paper_title: IndoNutriQA: An Indonesian Clinical Nutrition Question Answering Benchmark

title: Automated screening of privacy risks in medical AI
authors: Konstantinos Vrettos, Eleftherios Tzanis, Haridimos Kondylakis, Evangelia E. Vassalou, Florence X. Doo, Michail E. Klontzas
abstract: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) models are often shared without their training data, assuming this protects the patients who contributed them. However, a model can reveal whether a patient's records were used in training, a privacy breach known as a membership inference attack. This risk is usually reported as a cohort average, which can appear negligible while individual patients are almost certainly exposed. Identifying potentially vulnerable records before developing a production model could make privacy assessment more practical. We measured each patient's vulnerability to membership inference attack, across 7,789 models trained on six clinical datasets in four modalities, including two adapted pretrained medical models. Training choices changed how many patients had high attack scores, but the patients who ranked highest by risk largely stayed the same across the configurations we tested. Stronger weight decay reduced the exposed cohort up to threefold, yet largely the same patients remained most at risk across training recipes, architectures and initializations, including foundation models. Therefore, we developed a lightweight screening tool that uses four small models to identify patients with high risk of exposure before production-model training. We also assessed if flagged patients could be protected without removing their data. Privacy screening should become incorporated into data preparation for clinical AI.

infographic.key_insight: Patients at highest risk of training-data membership inference largely remained the same across tested models, enabling early screening with four small models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Screening before production-model training could help clinical AI teams identify privacy risks that cohort-average metrics may hide.
method: Measured patient-level vulnerability to membership inference attacks.
Compared risk rankings across training recipes, architectures and initializations.
Developed a four-model screening tool and assessed protection without removing flagged records.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study evaluated 7,789 models across six clinical datasets and four modalities, including two adapted pretrained medical models; stronger weight decay reduced the exposed cohort by up to threefold.
infographic.watch_item: Screening flags potential vulnerability rather than guaranteeing privacy, and its reliability beyond the tested datasets and configurations remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Automated screening of privacy risks in medical AI

title: Hair Segmentation and Skin Characterization on Macroscopic Dermatological Images for Laser Treatment Parameterization
authors: Alex Navarro Navarro, Marc Arriaga Hidalgo, Carlos Moreno Rubio, Maxime Talarmain, Noelia Vaquero Gallardo
abstract: Current light-based devices, such as laser hair removal, intense pulsed light (IPL), vascular laser therapy, and dermatologic phototherapy, are widely used in clinical dermatology but rely heavily on subjective manual parameterization or uncalibrated point-based colorimeters. To overcome these limitations, this work presents a unified system for hair segmentation and skin characterization in macroscopic dermatological images. Unlike most existing literature that relies on dermoscopic datasets captured under highly controlled conditions, our approach is specifically designed for macroscopic images that replicate real clinical laser treatments. The proposed pipeline integrates a custom-trained variant of the YOLOv9 deep learning architecture for instance segmentation and classical image processing within a single workflow to extract objective skin and hair parameters such as phototype, hair density, color, and thickness. A color calibration stage using spectrophotometric measurements ensures accurate feature estimation regardless of illumination conditions. Experimental results show competitive segmentation metrics (mAP@50 $\approx$ 0.80) on a custom dataset featuring short, shaved hairs, typical of pre-treatment scenarios. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed pipeline in providing the objective, foundational skin and hair features required for future automated laser parameterization, paving the way for its extension to broader light-based medical therapies.

infographic.key_insight: A unified AI pipeline segments hair and estimates skin and hair characteristics from macroscopic dermatological images to support future laser treatment parameterization.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Objective measurements could help reduce reliance on subjective assessment, but automated treatment settings and clinical benefits remain unvalidated.
method: Custom-trained YOLOv9 variant for hair instance segmentation.
Classical image processing to estimate phototype, hair density, color, and thickness.
Spectrophotometric color calibration to account for illumination differences.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a custom dataset featuring short, shaved hairs typical of pre-treatment images, segmentation achieved mAP@50 of approximately 0.80.
infographic.watch_item: Generalizability across skin tones, imaging conditions, and clinical settings is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Hair Segmentation and Skin Characterization on Macroscopic Dermatological Images for Laser Treatment Parameterization

title: Detection and Validation of Hidden Subgroup Disparities in Clinical AI
authors: Alceu Bissoto, Trung-Dung Hoang, Tim Flühmann, Nina Weng, Susu Sun, Christian F. Baumgartner
abstract: Machine learning (ML) models used in clinical workflows often perform systematically differently across patient groups, raising concerns about equity and patient safety. Traditional subgroup analyses can expose such disparities only when rich metadata (e.g., patient demographics) is available and captures the sources of performance variation, conditions rarely met in practice. Algorithmic subgroup discovery methods offer a solution by identifying coherent groups from learned feature representations, but because true underlying stratifications are unknown, these methods are hard to evaluate. As a result, subgroup discovery has not been systematically applied or assessed for performance monitoring. Our main objective is to evaluate algorithmic subgroup discovery for performance monitoring, assessing the discovered subgroups' performance gaps and semantic coherence. Investigating cardiomegaly classification in a dataset of 223,228 chest X-rays, we showed that the discovered subgroups exhibited larger performance gaps (accuracies of 0.61-0.90) than traditional metadata-based analysis (0.80-0.94) and were frequently interpretable using patient, acquisition, and model metadata. As a proof of concept, we also showed that annotations from learned subgroups can be used to mitigate the biases they expose. We conclude that subgroup discovery is a practical and effective tool to enhance the performance validation and monitoring of ML systems in healthcare.

infographic.key_insight: Algorithmic subgroup discovery revealed hidden accuracy disparities in a cardiomegaly classifier that traditional metadata-based analyses did not fully capture.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Finding underperforming patient groups could strengthen clinical AI validation and monitoring for equity and safety.
method: Identify coherent subgroups from learned feature representations.
Compare subgroup performance gaps with metadata-based analyses and assess interpretability.
Test learned subgroup annotations for bias mitigation as a proof of concept.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 223,228 chest X-rays, discovered subgroups had accuracies of 0.61–0.90 versus 0.80–0.94 for metadata-defined groups and were frequently interpretable using patient, acquisition, and model metadata.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence comes from one imaging task; generalizability and prospective monitoring benefits require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Detection and Validation of Hidden Subgroup Disparities in Clinical AI

title: The LLENS Platform for On-Premises Large Language Model Agents in a Japanese University Hospital: Development and Evaluation Study
authors: Ken Enda, Jien Saito, Masami Mukai, Feng Han, Emir Turkes, Tatsumi Kusakabe
abstract: Large language model agents that use tools could take on part of the electronic health record and desk work that occupies physicians' time, but in many hospitals the medical information systems run inside closed networks, so the model and the agent harness must also sit inside. We designed, implemented, and deployed LLENS, a clinical support AI agent platform that runs inside the closed network of Hokkaido University Hospital on one host with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the open-weight model Kimi K2.6 (~1 trillion parameters), and a web application rebuilt from Open WebUI. The harness has 10 components, including page image reading, full-text attachment input, a path-addressed document tree without a vector index, a network-isolated sandbox, artifact return, self-checking of generated output, subagents, and saved procedures. Kimi K2.6 was chosen from 3 open-weight candidates and scored 480/500 on the 2026 Japanese Medical Licensing Examination; it generated 119 tokens/s for one user and served 16 concurrent requests at 908 tokens/s in total. On 180 questions over hospital documents (3 seeds each), mean accuracy was 10.7% with no documents, 81.3% with fixed retrieval (top 10 chunks of one lexical search), and 97.2% with interactive access, in which the model reads with document tools and the sandbox (15.9 percentage points above fixed retrieval, 95% CI 10.9-21.3); the difference lay in filtering/counting questions (16.7% vs 87.8%). Five scenarios with synthetic data ran on combinations of the components: needlestick injury response, batch adverse event grading, scanned referral letter transcription, falls data aggregation and plotting, and investigation of 3 topics by subagents. The platform has run on the hospital network since September 14, 2026.

infographic.key_insight: LLENS enabled an on-premises LLM agent to answer hospital-document questions with 97.2% accuracy using interactive tools, versus 81.3% with fixed retrieval.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The platform could support hospital document and administrative workflows inside closed networks, but patient-care benefits were not evaluated.
method: Deployed Kimi K2.6 on one server with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs inside a Japanese university hospital network.
Combined document-reading tools, a network-isolated sandbox, output self-checking, subagents, and saved procedures.
Compared document-access approaches and demonstrated five workflows using synthetic data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 180 hospital-document questions evaluated with 3 seeds each, interactive access outperformed fixed retrieval by 15.9 percentage points (95% CI 10.9–21.3).
infographic.watch_item: Document-question accuracy and synthetic demonstrations do not establish clinical safety or real-world workload reduction; the reported hardware requirements are substantial.
infographic.paper_title: The LLENS Platform for On-Premises Large Language Model Agents in a Japanese University Hospital: Development and Evaluation Study

title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge
authors: Min Zeng, Zaifu Zhan, Kai Yu, Rui Zhang
abstract: Medical knowledge evolves as clinical guidelines revise recommendations, yet whether large language models (LLMs) faithfully incorporate such changes remains unclear. We introduce ChronoEvo, comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from incorporation into clinical recommendations. In the primary model, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions and 80.2% were clinically correct, but only 58.5% fully incorporated guidance, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point recognition-incorporation gap. This dissociation persisted across 14 models and was corroborated by two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses, yielding a 40.3-percentage-point gap in the validation sample. Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were associated with retention of outdated guidance. A revision-salience intervention reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness but did not significantly improve full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of evolving medical knowledge as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability, even when updated guideline evidence is available.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs can recognize updated medical guidance without fully incorporating it into recommendations: the primary model showed a 32.3-percentage-point gap.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Providing updated guideline evidence may not prevent LLMs from retaining outdated recommendations, raising reliability concerns for clinical use.
method: Introduced ChronoEvo: 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 types of medical knowledge change.
Evaluated recognition versus incorporation across 14 models, with two-clinician adjudication of 300 responses.
Tested a revision-salience intervention to emphasize updated guidance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The primary model recognized 90.8% of revisions but fully incorporated 58.5%; clinician-adjudicated validation found a 40.3-percentage-point recognition–incorporation gap.
infographic.watch_item: Emphasizing revisions reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness, but did not significantly improve full incorporation.
infographic.paper_title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge

title: PathJev: Decision-Native Vision-Language Modelling for Histopathology
authors: Cristian Tommasino, Antonio M. Rinaldi
abstract: Vision-language models used for decisions in histopathology rarely return calibrated probabilities over the candidates a user cares about. Decision-native models write a question and a candidate set chosen at run time into the input and return a normalised distribution from a small decision head in one forward pass. We build PathJev-P, a decision-native model for histopathology: MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head, trained on 40,000 patch states from three public collections whose expert labels are turned into typed questions with organ-specific candidate sets and a "none of these" option. In a comparison over 3 seeds with an analysis plan fixed before testing, on test sets without documented overlap with the training data of the backbone, PathJev-P is more accurate than a generative model trained with the same backbone, data and selection rule, the zero-shot pathology model CONCH and a general medical decision model (balanced accuracy 0.541 against 0.492, 0.345 and 0.213); its advantage over the generative model comes from two organs absent from training. The calibration advantage depends on how the generative model's probabilities are read out. With the summed candidate log-likelihood used in previous work, PathJev-P has the lower calibration error (ECE 0.204 against 0.279); with a length-normalised read-out of the same generative model, examined post hoc, the two have similar mean calibration error (0.201) and the generative model is better calibrated on the unseen organs, where PathJev-P remains over-confident. A supervised linear probe on a pathology foundation model is better calibrated in every setting. In a qualitative whole-slide demonstration, PathJev-P labels unsupervised tissue clusters with abstention and separates carcinoma from other tissue while running the model on a fraction of the tiles.

infographic.key_insight: PathJev-P improved histopathology classification accuracy over tested comparators, but its calibration advantage depended on how generative-model probabilities were calculated.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Probabilities over user-selected tissue categories, including “none of these,” could support pathology research workflows, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Adapted MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a small decision head.
Trained on 40,000 patch states from three public collections using organ-specific questions and candidate sets.
Returned normalized candidate probabilities in one forward pass; qualitatively demonstrated whole-slide cluster labeling with abstention.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three seeds with a prespecified analysis plan, balanced accuracy was 0.541 versus 0.492 for a matched generative model, 0.345 for CONCH and 0.213 for a general medical decision model.
infographic.watch_item: PathJev-P remained overconfident on organs absent from training, and a supervised pathology linear probe was better calibrated in every evaluated setting.
infographic.paper_title: PathJev: Decision-Native Vision-Language Modelling for Histopathology

title: ALLMTS: Automated LLM-based Medical Triage System
authors: Michał Remigiusz Janiszewski, Artur Stopa, Łukasz Lenkiewicz, Wojciech Achtelik, Bartosz Gonczarek
abstract: Telephone triage is a safety critical task: from a brief intake note, a nurse must decide whether a caller needs an ambulance, an emergency department, an appointment, or self care at home. Queried directly, large language models (LLMs) are unreliable: they over-escalate routine cases and cannot justify their recommendations against an auditable clinical standard. We present the Automated LLM-based Medical Triage System (ALLMTS), which grounds every disposition in the same commercially maintained telehealth guidelines nurses use. Rather than asking an LLM to triage, ALLMTS makes it execute the guideline: it selects the appropriate guideline and evaluates its triage assessment questions. The disposition follows deterministically from the first positive answer, using the same traversal rule a nurse follows. We evaluate ALLMTS on 566 synthetic, expert-validated scenarios spanning 14 dispositions and designed to test specific guideline questions. ALLMTS achieves 0.95 accuracy, compared with 0.47 for a raw-LLM baseline. On a curated 50-scenario subset released as an open benchmark, ALLMTS reaches 0.98 accuracy, on par with the 0.944 correct disposition rate that a five nurse expert panel recorded on those same scenarios. Critically, on that subset the baselines have over-triage rates of up to 0.50 (0.44 on the full dataset), whereas ALLMTS reduces the over-triage rate to at most 0.02 while maintaining low under-triage. These results support coupling LLM language understanding with executable clinical guidelines for triage from intake notes.

infographic.key_insight: ALLMTS grounds LLM-based triage in executable clinical guidelines, achieving 95% accuracy versus 47% for a raw-LLM baseline on synthetic scenarios.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Guideline-based automation could support more consistent, auditable telephone triage while reducing unnecessary escalation.
method: Selects a commercially maintained telehealth guideline from an intake note.
Uses an LLM to evaluate the guideline’s triage assessment questions.
Determines disposition using the guideline’s first-positive-answer traversal rule.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered 566 synthetic, expert-validated scenarios across 14 dispositions; on a curated 50-scenario subset, accuracy was 98% versus 94.4% for a five-nurse panel.
infographic.watch_item: Synthetic-scenario results do not establish real-world safety; prospective validation is needed before clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: ALLMTS: Automated LLM-based Medical Triage System

title: Decoupling Patient Personas and Clinical Workflows: A Dual-Agent Approach to Realistic Medical Dialogue Generation
authors: Qiyuan Li, Xiaomei Guo, Chao Gao, Haijiang Liu, Deyu Chen, Caicai Guo
abstract: Pre-consultation medical dialogues are essential for collecting comprehensive patient information, but are costly to obtain at scale due to privacy and ethical constraints. Existing LLM-based synthesis methods often rely on prompt engineering or rigid rules, limiting their ability to balance clinical relevance with realistic patient diversity. We propose CoRPS-Dial, a controllable dual-agent framework for pre-consultation medical dialogue synthesis that integrates patient personas with guideline-aligned clinical workflow rules. CoRPS-Dial generates dialogues through interactions between a persona-driven patient agent and a process-guided doctor agent, followed by post-hoc quality control for role consistency, workflow completeness, and textual consistency. Experiments on coronary heart disease demonstrate that CoRPS-Dial improves alignment between synthetic and real dialogues in information coverage, clinical compliance, and dialogue naturalness. Downstream fine-tuning experiments further confirm the utility of the generated synthetic data for medical dialogue tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of CoRPS-Dial for clinically grounded and controllable medical dialogue synthesis.

infographic.key_insight: CoRPS-Dial separates patient personas from clinical workflows to generate realistic, controllable pre-consultation medical dialogues.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support training medical dialogue systems when access to real patient conversations is constrained by privacy and ethical concerns.
method: Pair a persona-driven patient agent with a process-guided doctor agent.
Guide conversations with guideline-aligned clinical workflow rules.
Apply post-hoc checks for role consistency, workflow completeness, and textual consistency.
infographic.evidence_signal: In coronary heart disease experiments, the authors report improved alignment with real dialogues in information coverage, clinical compliance, and naturalness, plus benefits for downstream fine-tuning; the abstract provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Generalizability beyond coronary heart disease and safety in real clinical use remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Decoupling Patient Personas and Clinical Workflows: A Dual-Agent Approach to Realistic Medical Dialogue Generation

title: Deep Learning-Based Prediction of HER2 Status from Whole-Brain MRI in Breast Cancer Brain Metastases
authors: Sara Early, Chris Kang, Vibujithan Vigneshwaran, Kimberly Amador, Roger Y. Tsang, Nils D. Forkert
abstract: Purpose: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status is a key biomarker relevant for prognostication and treatment decision making in metastatic breast cancer. Thus, the aim of this work was to explore whether HER2 status can be predicted directly from whole-brain post-contrast T1-weighted (T1w) MRI scans in breast cancer brain metastases (BCBM) using deep learning, and whether providing explicit tumour segmentation information improves prediction. Methods: Using the publicly available BCBM-Radiogenomics dataset, we analysed 135 patients, including 70 HER2+ and 65 HER2- patients. Three approaches were implemented and evaluated: a conventional radiomics model, a simple fully convolutional network (SFCN) using T1w MRI scans alone, and an SFCN using T1w MRI scans with an expert-derived tumour mask as an additional input channel. Results: The radiomics model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.602 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.528--0.677) while the SFCN achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.667 (95% CI, 0.63--0.71) using T1w MRI scans alone, which increased to 0.692 (95% CI, 0.58--0.81) when an explicit tumour mask was additionally provided. Conclusion: However, the modest performance across all approaches demonstrates the difficulty of predicting HER2 status from structural MRI scans alone. The difference between the segmentation-free and mask-guided SFCN models suggests that much of the predictive signal captured by the deep-learning model may be learned directly from whole-brain T1w MRI without requiring explicit tumour delineation. These findings support further investigation of segmentation-free deep-learning approaches as a potential non-invasive strategy to support HER2 status determination in BCBM.

infographic.key_insight: Whole-brain MRI deep learning showed modest HER2 prediction performance, with ROC-AUC increasing from 0.667 to 0.692 when expert tumour masks were added.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This exploratory approach could support future non-invasive HER2 assessment in breast cancer brain metastases but is not established for clinical decision-making.
method: Analysed post-contrast T1-weighted brain MRI from the public BCBM-Radiogenomics dataset.
Compared conventional radiomics with a simple fully convolutional network.
Tested the network with MRI alone and with an additional expert-derived tumour mask.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 135 patients (70 HER2-positive, 65 HER2-negative), ROC-AUC was 0.602 for radiomics, 0.667 for MRI-only deep learning, and 0.692 for mask-guided deep learning.
infographic.watch_item: Modest performance and overlapping confidence intervals leave the benefit of tumour masks uncertain; broader validation is needed.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Learning-Based Prediction of HER2 Status from Whole-Brain MRI in Breast Cancer Brain Metastases
